title: An identity-provider account takes over an administrator past an enrolled second factor, and deactivating that administrator does not take the access away

steps.action: sign in through the workspace's OAuth provider from an identity-provider account whose profile carries the administrator's email address, which the provider never claims to have verified
steps.result: the identity melded into the administrator's local account, a login code in the callback URL, and the administrator's own password reset, which locks the real owner out

steps.action: redeem that login code although the account has TOTP enrolled, because on the OAuth path the second-factor decision is the account's age rather than its enrolled methods
steps.result: a full administrator session with no code ever demanded: rooms.adminRooms answers HTTP 200 while the same account's password login answers totp-required

steps.action: after the operator deactivates the compromised administrator, which deletes every one of its tokens, sign in through the same provider again and redeem a new login code
steps.result: a working token for the deactivated administrator: /api/v1/me reports active false and rooms.adminRooms still answers HTTP 200, while the password path refuses the account

combined_impact: Proven in the lab: an outsider whose only asset was an identity-provider account that can set its own email address obtained a full administrator session on a TOTP-enrolled administrator with no second factor, reset that administrator's password in the process, and kept administrative access after the operator performed the documented response to a compromise. Attacker capability before: an account at a trusted identity provider. After: workspace administration, with the owner locked out of their own account and with the three responses an operator reaches for (reset the password, rely on 2FA, deactivate the account) all ineffective; only deleting the account or stripping its roles ends it. Blast radius: the whole workspace, since the account reached is an administrator.
preconditions: An OAuth login provider enabled whose users can set their own profile email address without proving ownership (a self-managed GitLab, a custom OIDC provider, any provider with a self-service address), and an account at it. This is the business configuration the chain is conditional on; the run enables Rocket.Chat's built-in GitLab backend against a stand-in provider and restores the settings. Step 2 additionally needs the victim administrator to be inside the Accounts_TwoFactorAuthentication_RememberFor window (1800 seconds by default), which is where a freshly provisioned administrator lives; outside it the chain stops at the 2FA challenge and the password reset and the IdP link still stand.
fix_order: Fix step 1: in the meld (accounts_meld.js:14-31, VULN-002) link an identity-provider identity to an existing local account only on a verified-email claim, and never on the address alone. One change breaks the chain, because steps 2 and 3 both act on the account the meld attached the attacker to. Side effect: removes a convenience for some deployments: users whose provider does not assert email verification are no longer linked automatically to an existing local account, so an administrator links them by hand or the user signs in with their password once; nothing changes for providers that do assert it. The account-state hole (VULN-030) still deserves its own fix, since it makes deactivation ineffective for every other way an account can be linked to a provider.
